title: How Can A Disabled Person Get Help For House Cleaning?
summary: Discover how disabled individuals can get house cleaning help with GoGoGrandparent—simplifying home services for seniors, elderly, and disabled people.
body_markdown:
There are four main ways to get help with house cleaning for people living with disabilities: family and community support, state-funded programs such as Medicaid home and community based services, nonprofit or volunteer cleaning programs, and hiring a cleaner or using a home services provider like GoGoGrandparent that arranges a vetted cleaner for you. Several cost nothing. The hard part is usually not finding cleaning help, it's knowing which door to knock on first.


If housework has started to feel like more than you can manage, you're in good company.[More than 1 in 4 U.S. adults have some type of disability](https://www.cdc.gov/disability-and-health/articles-documents/disability-impacts-all-of-us-infographic.html) , according to the CDC, and 12.2% of adults have a mobility disability specifically. Plenty of those people run their own households. They've just changed how some of it gets done.


## **Why does house cleaning matter more than it looks?**


A clean home isn't only about appearances. Cleaning affects your safety, your health, and how comfortable you feel in your own space.


A cluttered floor is a fall risk.[Over 14 million older adults, about 1 in 4, report falling every year](https://www.cdc.gov/falls/data-research/index.html) , and the CDC lists falls as the leading cause of injury-related death for adults over 65. Loose rugs, a cord across a hallway, a stack of boxes in the spare room. Dust and pet dander can make respiratory symptoms harder to manage too.


There's also the part nobody puts in a brochure. Living in a home you can't keep the way you'd like wears on you. That isn't vanity, it's your own space not feeling like yours.


## **What are your options for getting cleaning help?**


Four realistic routes exist, and most people end up combining two of them.


- **Family, friends, and neighbors.** Free, and often fastest to arrange. The catch is that it runs on somebody else's schedule, and asking repeatedly gets uncomfortable even when the person is happy to help.
- **State and federal programs.** Medicaid home and community based services, state waiver programs, and Veterans Affairs benefits can cover homemaker help and light housekeeping for people who qualify. The coverage is real, but so is the paperwork.
- **Nonprofit and volunteer programs.** Faith groups, disability resource centers, and local charities sometimes run free or low-cost cleaning days, though coverage varies enormously by town.
- **A cleaner, or a service that arranges one for you.** The most predictable option, since you pick the schedule. The work is in finding someone trustworthy, which is where[GoGo Home Services](https://www.gogograndparent.com/services/home-services-for-seniors) saves real effort: you call, and GoGo arranges the cleaning for you.


## **What do government programs actually cover?**


The short answer is that it depends, and it depends more on your state than on you.


Medicaid's home and community based services are the main route. Many state programs can pay for a homemaker to help with light housekeeping, laundry, and similar tasks, usually as part of a broader care plan rather than as a standalone cleaning service. A few things worth knowing:


- **It's usually tied to personal care, not cleaning alone.** Programs tend to fund housekeeping as part of helping someone stay safely at home, so an assessment normally looks at daily living tasks as a whole.
- **There can be a wait.**[Forty-one states keep waiting lists](https://www.kff.org/medicaid/a-look-at-waiting-lists-for-medicaid-home-and-community-based-services-from-2016-to-2025/) for these services. In 2025, older adults and people with physical disabilities waited an average of 15 months. Apply before the need becomes urgent rather than after.
- **Veterans have a separate route.** If you or your spouse served, VA programs are worth asking about directly rather than assuming Medicaid is the only door.


The practical first step is your local **Area Agency on Aging** , which can tell you what your state offers. You can find yours through the **Eldercare Locator** at eldercare.acl.gov, a free service from the U.S. Administration for Community Living. Because these programs can take months, many people arrange cleaning through GoGo in the meantime and keep the application running alongside it.


## **Which cleaning jobs should you hand over first?**


If you're going to get help, it pays to be deliberate about which cleaning jobs go first.


1. **Anything at floor level.** Scrubbing a bathtub, mopping, cleaning under furniture. Getting down is manageable for many people; getting back up is usually the harder half.
2. **Anything overhead.** Light fixtures, the tops of cabinets, changing a smoke alarm battery. Reaching overhead can shift your balance, especially on a step stool.
3. **Anything heavy or awkward.** Wet mop buckets, full laundry baskets on stairs, moving a couch to vacuum behind it.
4. **Anything you've started putting off.** The chore you keep rescheduling is often the one that has quietly become too hard.


Keep the jobs you still enjoy and can do safely: wiping down a counter, folding laundry at a table, sorting the mail.

## **How do you choose a cleaning service you can trust?**


Whoever you go with, a few questions separate a good arrangement from one you'll regret.


- **Are the cleaners insured and background checked?** Ask directly, and ask who actually employs them.
- **Is it the same person each time?** Consistency matters more than people expect, especially if explaining your setup takes effort.
- **Will they work around your equipment and your routine?** A good cleaner adapts to a walker in the hallway or a shower chair that stays put.
- **Can you start small?** One visit gives you a chance to see whether the cleaner and the schedule feel right before committing to anything ongoing.


If you'd rather not run that search yourself, GoGo Home Services answers most of these questions for you, because the home services team screens the providers before they reach your door.


## **Staying in your own home, on your own terms**


Getting help with housework isn't giving something up. Handing over the cleaning jobs that have become risky is often what makes staying in your own home possible for years longer. The goal was never to do everything yourself. It's to keep the home you want and stay in charge of how it runs. If you want help arranging it, GoGoGrandparent is a phone call away on1 (855) 464-6872 .


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **How can a disabled person get help for house cleaning?**


There are four main routes: family and community support, state programs such as Medicaid home and community based services, nonprofit or volunteer cleaning programs, and hiring a cleaner or using a service like GoGoGrandparent that arranges one for you. Your local Area Agency on Aging can tell you which programs you qualify for in your state.


### **Does Medicaid pay for house cleaning?**


In many states, Medicaid home and community based services can cover a homemaker to help with light housekeeping and laundry, usually as part of a wider care plan rather than as cleaning on its own. Eligibility and covered tasks vary by state, and some programs have waiting lists, so check with your state's Medicaid office or your Area Agency on Aging.


### **Are there free house cleaning services for adults living with disabilities?**


Sometimes. Faith groups, disability resource centers, and local charities occasionally run free or low-cost cleaning programs, and state-funded homemaker help costs nothing to those who qualify. Availability depends heavily on where you live, which is why the Area Agency on Aging is the right first call.


### **What cleaning tasks are most dangerous to keep doing?**


Anything at floor level, anything overhead, and anything heavy. Scrubbing a tub, reaching above your head, and carrying wet mop buckets or full laundry baskets are the jobs most often behind a fall. Those are the ones worth handing over first.


### **Can a family member arrange cleaning help on my behalf?**


Yes, once they've been added to your account as someone who can make requests. A son, daughter, or other family member can then arrange the cleaning, including from another state, and stay involved in scheduling afterwards.


### **How do I know if a cleaning service is trustworthy?**


Ask whether cleaners are insured and background checked, who employs them, whether you'll get the same person each visit, and how the company handles problems. Starting with a single clean rather than a standing schedule is a low-risk way to find out.
